summary: RFC 5440 defines the Include Route Object in PCEP to specify network elements a computed path must traverse, but does not say whether its subobject list is ordered. This standards-track RFC clarifies that.

eli5.summary: A route request lists places to pass through, but not whether in order. This settles it.

questions: is the pcep include route object ordered
what does the l bit mean in an iro
subtitle: PCEP's Include Route Object is now an ordered list, and its L bit marks loose versus strict hops.

tldr.problem: RFC 5440 defines the Include Route Object (IRO) but does not say whether its subobjects are ordered, and says the L bit has no meaning in an IRO.
tldr.mechanism: This update says an IRO is an ordered list of subobjects representing abstract nodes, and that the L bit is set for a loose hop and clear for a strict hop, as in RFC 3209.
tldr.outcome: Implementations that always treated IRO hops as loose may interwork badly with conforming ones, so the RFC describes the possible effects.

today: RFC 7896 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5440. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: The Ambiguity in the IRO
sections.content:
In the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP), a Path Computation Client (PCC) asks a PCE to compute a path. RFC 5440 defines the Include Route Object (IRO) to name network elements the path must traverse, but does not say whether it is an ordered or unordered list, and defines the L bit as having no meaning within an IRO.

RFC 5441 uses an IRO to indicate the sequence of domains in inter-domain path computation, so a standard representation was needed for interoperability. This document updates Section 7.12 of RFC 5440.
sections.eli5: A list of stops needs to say whether the order matters. This RFC says it does.

sections.title: What Changes in RFC 5440
sections.content:
The last line of Section 7.12 of RFC 5440, "The L bit of such sub-object has no meaning within an IRO", is removed. Two statements are added to the first paragraph.

  • The content of an IRO is an ordered list of subobjects representing a series of abstract nodes (see Section 4.3.2 of RFC 3209).
  • The L bit is set if the subobject represents a loose hop. If it is not set, the subobject is a strict hop, interpreted as in Section 4.3.3.1 of RFC 3209.
sections.eli5: Stops are visited in the order listed, and each is marked either "must go exactly here" or "somewhere around here is fine".

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Because RFC 5440 was unclear, some implementations may always treat IRO subobjects as loose. Two mismatches are described.

  • A non-conforming PCC sends an IRO to a conforming PCE: the PCE may unexpectedly fail to find a path, because it reads the hops as strict while the PCC thinks of them as loose.
  • A conforming PCC sends strict hops to a non-conforming PCE: the PCE may return a path that does not comply, and the PCC may notice or may end up using an incorrect path.
sections.eli5: If one side thinks a stop is flexible and the other thinks it is exact, the trip may fail or go the wrong way.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The update introduces no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 5440. The RFC adds that PCEP operates over TCP and points to RFC 6952 for an analysis of security issues for routing protocols that use TCP.
sections.eli5: Clarifying the rules does not open any new doors for trouble.

Awduche, D., et al., "RSVP-TE: Extensions to RSVP for LSP Tunnels", RFC 3209, December 2001.
Vasseur, JP., Ed., et al., "A Backward-Recursive PCE-Based Computation (BRPC) Procedure to Compute Shortest Constrained Inter-Domain Traffic Engineering Label Switched Paths", RFC 5441, April 2009.
